title: Controllers, DTOs, and Validation
summary: Map HTTP requests to controller methods, accept and return records instead of entities, and reject bad input with Bean Validation and problem responses.
intro: The controller is the front door of your API, and most tickets you pick up add or change one. Reviewers look for the same things every time: the right status codes, request bodies that are checked before any rule runs, and no database entity leaking into a response. In this lesson you read shopfront's product and order endpoints, their request and response records, and the handler that gives every error the same JSON shape.

steps.title: Mapping requests to methods
steps.body:
A class marked `@RestController` turns HTTP requests into method calls and writes each method's return value as JSON. Annotations describe the mapping:

| Annotation | What it maps |
| --- | --- |
| `@RequestMapping("/api/products")` | The base path for every method in the class |
| `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@DeleteMapping` | The HTTP method, plus the rest of the path |
| `@PathVariable String sku` | The `{sku}` part of the path |
| `@RequestParam` | A query parameter, optional with `required = false` or a `defaultValue` |
| `@RequestBody` | The JSON body, read into a record |

Return a record for a 200. Return a `ResponseEntity` when you need another status or a header, like 201 with a `Location`, and use `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)` for a 204 with no body. A good controller method is a few lines long: read the request, call one service method, pick the status. It never touches a repository and never holds a business rule.

examples.title: Reading products
examples.prompt: The read side of the catalog, and its answer to `GET /api/products?category=kitchen&inStock=true&size=2`.
examples.explanation: `search` takes three optional filters and a `Pageable`, which Spring Data fills from `page`, `size`, and `sort`, so `?sort=priceCents,desc` works with no parsing code. `@PageableDefault` sets the defaults, and `max-page-size: 50` in `application.yml` caps what a client can ask for. Wrapping the page in `PagedModel` gives the JSON a stable shape, the items in `content` and the numbers in `page`, which clients use to draw pagination. `get` returns a `ProductResponse` record, and Spring writes it with a 200.

examples.title: Writing products
examples.prompt: The write side, and what an admin gets back from `POST /api/products` for a new salad spinner.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 201
Location: /api/products/KT-007

{
  "sku": "KT-007",
  "name": "Salad Spinner",
  "description": "Dries greens in seconds.",
  "priceCents": 2299,
  "stock": 12,
  "category": "kitchen",
  "active": true
}
examples.explanation: `create` answers 201 with a `Location` header that points at the new product, which is what clients and HTTP tools expect after a POST. `update` uses PUT, so the body carries the whole product. `delete` answers 204 with no body, and only takes the product off sale, because past orders still point at it. Notice what is missing: no SQL, no stock rules, and no role checks. `SecurityConfig` decides who may call these routes before the method runs, and `CatalogService` holds the rules.

steps.title: Records in, records out
steps.body:
The JSON your API accepts and returns is a contract with every client, so give it its own types, called DTOs (data transfer objects). Write them as Java records: a record declares its fields once and gets a constructor, accessors like `sku()`, `equals`, and `toString` for free, and Jackson reads and writes records directly.

Never accept or return an entity. An entity mirrors a table, so returning one sends every column, `password_hash` included, and ties your API to your schema. Reading one from a request is worse: a client could set fields you never meant to expose, like `role` or `stock`.

Shopfront keeps request and response records in each feature's `dto/` package. Each response record has a static `from(entity)` factory, so the mapping lives in one place.

examples.title: A request record
examples.prompt: The body of `POST /api/products` and `PUT /api/products/{sku}`, with its constraints and defaults.
examples.explanation: The numbers are `Long` and `Integer`, not `long` and `int`. Spring Boot 4 ships Jackson 3, which refuses to put a missing value into a primitive and answers 400 with a parse error before validation runs. With wrapper types, a missing `stock` arrives as `null`, and `@NotNull` reports it with a clear message like any other field. The compact constructor, the block without a parameter list, runs before the fields are set. It fills in defaults for the optional `description` and `active`, so the service never sees a null there.

examples.title: A response record
examples.prompt: What `GET /api/customers/me` returns for ana, and the record that decides its shape. The `Customer` entity behind it also has a `passwordHash`.
examples.explanation: The record lists exactly the five fields clients may see, so the hash cannot slip out, even when someone adds a column to the entity later. `from` is the one place that maps the entity to this shape, and services call it while their transaction is still open, so anything it reads is loaded safely. `Instant` becomes an ISO-8601 string and the `Role` enum becomes its name, which is what JSON clients expect.

steps.title: Validation and error responses
steps.body:
Check the shape of the input at the edge, before any rule runs. Bean Validation puts the rules on the record itself, with annotations like `@NotNull`, `@NotBlank`, `@Size`, `@Positive`, `@Max`, `@Email`, and `@Pattern`. `@Valid` on a `@RequestBody` parameter makes Spring check them, and a failure answers 400 before your method is called. Constraints on `@RequestParam` and `@PathVariable` parameters are checked too.

Clients need every error in one shape. Spring supports RFC 9457 problem details: JSON with `title`, `status`, `detail`, and `instance`, sent as `application/problem+json`. One `@RestControllerAdvice` class turns every exception into a problem, so services only throw `NotFoundException`, `ConflictException`, or `UnprocessableException` and never build a response.

Shopfront draws a useful line. A request with the wrong shape is 400, from validation. A well-formed request the shop cannot use, like an unknown SKU, is 422 from a service, and one that clashes with the current state, like no stock left, is 409.

examples.title: Checking every line of an order
examples.prompt: One line of `POST /api/orders`, which holds its lines in a `List<@Valid @NotNull LineRequest>`. The output answers a body with two bad lines.
examples.explanation: `@Valid` on the list's element type tells the validator to check inside every line, so errors come back with paths like `lines[0].quantity`. Every broken field is reported at once, sorted by path, so a client can show all the problems in one go. The `message` on `@Pattern` replaces the default text, which would print the raw regular expression. The `errors` map is not built in: `ApiExceptionHandler` adds it. Validation only checks the shape. Whether `BK-001` is really for sale is the service's job.

examples.title: One place for errors
examples.prompt: Parts of shopfront's exception handler, and its answer when bob orders a SKU the shop does not sell.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 422

{
  "detail": "No product with SKU ZZ-999 is for sale.",
  "instance": "/api/orders",
  "status": 422,
  "title": "Unknown product",
  "sku": "ZZ-999"
}
examples.explanation: `@RestControllerAdvice` applies to every controller. Each `@ExceptionHandler` method maps one exception type to a `ProblemDetail`, and Spring writes it with the status and the `application/problem+json` content type. The `sku` field comes from the exception's properties, so a client can highlight the line that failed. Extending `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` keeps Spring's own answers for bad JSON, wrong types, and unknown URLs. The catch-all for `Exception` logs anything unexpected once, with its stack trace, and answers a plain 500, so no stack trace or SQL ever reaches a client.

recap:
- A `@RestController` maps routes to methods. Keep each method short: read the request, call one service method, pick the status.
- Return a record for 200, `ResponseEntity.created(uri)` for 201 with a `Location`, and `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)` for 204.
- Accept and return records, never entities. Use wrapper types for numbers, since Jackson 3 rejects a missing primitive.
- Put constraints on request records and `@Valid` on the parameter. A bad shape is 400, and a well-formed request the service refuses is 422 or 409.
- Turn every exception into an RFC 9457 problem in one `@RestControllerAdvice`, so services only throw.
